docs.title: Language Overview
docs.text:
The Jelly language was created for Siri Shortcuts because I was not satisfied with the GUI of Shortcuts. I wanted a way to write Shortcuts in a text-based language. That is why I created Jellycuts and the Jelly language.

The Jelly language is currently focused on creating a simple way to write Shortcuts without much hassle. The language is geared towards calling the Shortcuts actions as functions. However, in the future I plan to alter the way the language is interpreted so you are able to write code in a Swift or JavaScript-like fashion and have it translated into a Shortcut — or even write and compile it like any other language.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The first place to start is setting up your IDE. The current IDE for Jelly is the Jellycuts iOS App.

Once you have set up your IDE you can head over to Writing Your First Script to learn how to write your first Jellycut script.

docs.title: Downloading the iOS App
docs.text: If you have not already, you can get the Jellycuts iOS app from the App Store. After installing, run through the in-app tutorial to connect Jellycuts with Shortcuts and open the Starter Jellycut project.

docs.title: Let's get started
docs.text:
When you create a new project (or open Starter Jellycut) the first thing you will see is an import statement. This pulls in the Standard Shortcuts Library at a specific version. The next line is the metadata definition which tells Jellycuts details about how the Shortcut should be exported (for example its colour and icon).

import Shortcuts
#Color: red, #Icon: shortcuts

docs.title: Hello World!
docs.text:
Time for a classic 🖐🏻 Hello World.

  1. Add a Text block:

    jelly text(text: "Hello World!")

  2. Attach a Magic Variable so we can reference the output later:

    jelly text(text: "Hello World!") >> introduction

  3. Display it with an alert (showing String interpolation):

    jelly alert(alert: "${introduction}")

Putting it all together you get:

import Shortcuts
#Color: red, #Icon: shortcuts

text(text: "Hello World!") >> introduction
alert(alert: "${introduction}")

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Now that you have written your first Jellycut you can jump straight into creating more, or continue through the docs. A good next read is the Language Guide where you can learn the fundamentals.

docs.title: The Basics
docs.text: Jelly is an extremely simple language that pulls inspiration from Swift and JavaScript for most of its syntax. However, some parts of the language such as Metadata are Jelly-specific. If you already know one of these languages, learning Jelly should feel familiar. If you don’t, this guide will walk you through everything you need to know.

docs.title: How to go through this guide
docs.text: A good starting point is the tutorial Writing Your First Script in the Getting Started section. After you have written a simple script, come back here for topics you want to explore further.

docs.title: Declared Metadata
docs.text:
Metadata is optional for the Jelly language itself, but it is vital for the Jellycuts iOS app because it controls how a Jellycut is displayed when exported to Shortcuts.

Metadata is declared using a leading # followed by the tag name.

docs.title: Colour
docs.text:
Set the accent colour used for the exported Shortcut:

#Color: Red

Available colours: red, orange, tangerine, yellow, green, teal, lightblue, blue, navy, grape, purple, pink, grayblue, graygreen, graybrown.

docs.title: Icon
docs.text:
Choose the glyph shown on the exported Shortcut tile:

#Icon: Shortcuts

There are hundreds of icons. For convenience they are still listed in the legacy icon reference while we migrate the table into Markdown.

Tip: Declared metadata lines can be placed anywhere in your script, but they’re usually grouped together at the top for readability.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text: Strings are ubiquitous in Jelly — you’ll use them when calling functions and when setting variables.

docs.title: Basic string literal
docs.text: "String Content"

docs.title: Multiline string literal
docs.text:
"""
String Content
"""

docs.title: Variables inside a string
docs.text:
Insert a variable directly into a string using string interpolation:

"Hello ${username}"

docs.title: Escaping quotes
docs.text: If you need to include a double-quote (") inside your string, escape it with a backslash (\). The backslashes are automatically removed when the Jellycut is built.

docs.title: Traditional Variables
docs.text:
Variables in Jelly are mutable — their value can be changed after they’re created. A variable can hold values coming from:

  • A string
  • A number
  • A Magic Variable
  • A Global Variable

docs.title: Variable with a string value
docs.text: var HelloWorld = "Hello World"

docs.title: Multiline string value
docs.text:
var HelloWorldLong = """
Hello World!
I have multiple lines
"""

docs.title: Variable with a number value
docs.text: var MeaningOfLife = 42

docs.title: Variable with a Magic Variable value
docs.text:
Convert an existing magic variable into a traditional variable:

var MyVariable = FunctionOutput

docs.title: Variable with a Global Variable value
docs.text:
Global variables are read-only. To mutate their value assign them to a regular variable first:

var MutableGlobalVar = Shortcut Input

docs.title: Variables inside a string
docs.text: See the Strings guide for inserting variables into a string.

docs.title: Assignment after initialisation
docs.text:
// Initial value
var x = Shortcut Input

// New value
x = "Hello World!"
// or
var x = "Hello World!"

docs.title: Addition after initialisation
docs.text:
// Initial value
var x = Shortcut Input

// New value
x += "Hello World!"
// or
var x += "Hello World!"

Using += will turn the variable into an array, mirroring Shortcuts’ Add to Variable action.
